concepts.title: Fibre to Fabric: Classification of Fibres
concepts.definition: Every fabric begins as a fibre. Fibres classify into natural -- cotton, wool, silk, jute from plants and animals -- and man-made, further split into regenerated fibres like rayon and fully synthetic ones like polyester and nylon. Fibre properties decide what the finished cloth can do.
concepts.key_idea: Know the fibre, predict the fabric -- cotton breathes, wool warms, synthetics crease-resist.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe105.txt fibre sections (classification of fibres, natural and man made, regenerated and synthetic, cotton wool silk jute rayon polyester nylon)

solution_steps.explain: Cotton, wool, silk and jute grow in nature; rayon, polyester and nylon are manufactured.
Regenerated fibres rework natural cellulose into filament; synthetics are built entirely from chemicals.
Absorbency, strength, warmth and crease behaviour follow the fibre, guiding selection for use.

concepts.title: Yarns and Fabric Construction: Weaving and Knitting
concepts.definition: Fibres are spun into yarns, and yarns become fabric by two main routes: weaving, where lengthwise and crosswise yarns interlace at right angles, and knitting, where loops interlock. Woven cloth is stable and holds shape; knitted cloth stretches and yields.
concepts.key_idea: Interlaced yarns give stable cloth; interlocked loops give stretch -- construction is destiny for fabric.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe105.txt construction sections (yarn, weaving warp weft, knitting loops, woven versus knitted fabrics, other constructions)
question_patterns: distinguish weaving from knitting as methods of construction

solution_steps.explain: Short fibres are drawn and twisted into continuous yarns strong enough to build cloth.
In weaving, warp runs lengthwise and weft crosses it; plain, twill and satin are interlacing patterns.
Knitting interlocks loops in rows and courses; the loops give the stretch that wovens lack.

concepts.title: Finishes and Fabric Selection for Use
concepts.definition: Finishes alter fabric to fit its purpose -- bleaching, dyeing, printing for looks; starching, waterproofing, crease-resisting for performance. Selection means matching fibre, construction and finish to the end use, the wearer and the care the fabric can receive.
concepts.key_idea: Finishes dress the fabric for its job -- choose fibre, construction and finish together, not singly.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe105.txt finish and selection sections (bleaching dyeing printing, functional finishes, waterproofing crease resistance, selection criteria)

solution_steps.explain: Basic finishes clean and prepare; colouring finishes bleach, dye and print; functional finishes add crease-resistance, waterproofing or flame resistance.
Selection weighs fibre behaviour, construction strength and finish against cost and care facilities.
School wear wants durable, easily laundered cloth; ceremonies may prefer delicate, lustrous ones -- use rules the choice.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Sort into natural and man-made: cotton saree, polyester shirt, woollen sweater, rayon scarf, nylon rope.

solution_template.explain: Cotton saree and woollen sweater come from plant and animal sources.
Polyester shirt and nylon rope are fully synthetic; rayon scarf is man-made but regenerated from cellulose.
Within man-made, separate regenerated rayon from synthetic polyester and nylon.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A T-shirt stretches easily while a school shirt barely does. Explain the construction difference.

solution_template.explain: Its loops interlock -- a knitted construction -- so loops stretch and recover.
Its yarns interlace at right angles -- a woven construction -- which resists stretch.
Construction, not fibre alone, explains the behaviour difference.
